722.title: Ashvaghosha himself
722.hook: a brahmin-born poet and monk, remembered also for the poem of Nanda
722.howItsDone: Ashvaghosha's poems are read today in Sanskrit classes and in translation by students of Buddhism and of Indian literature, and the story of Nanda is retold in Buddhist teaching about craving and letting go.

segments.voice: Yesterday, final nirvana, and your line: the poem traveled. Did a good story go a little further through you? Today we turn from the poem to the person who wrote it. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

For weeks now, there's been a voice behind every scene. The king's fear in the palace. The worms in the plowed field. The gates swinging open without a sound. Mara's flowers. The long night under the tree. Someone chose every one of those pictures, and the words to hold them. That someone has a name, Ashvaghosha. And here's the honest part: we know very little about him. What we have is a short signature at the end of his poems, a handful of later stories, and the poems themselves.
screen: `A VOICE BEHIND EVERY SCENE.` → `HIS NAME: ASHVAGHOSHA.` → `WE KNOW VERY LITTLE.`

segments.voice: First, the signature. At the close of his other long poem, the author names himself: Ashvaghosha of Saketa, son of a woman named Suvarnakshi, a monk, a great poet and speaker. He tells us his town and his mother's name, and that he wore the robe. Not much more. Second, the brahmin. Later tradition says he was born a brahmin and trained in the old learning before he became a follower of the Buddha. His poems seem to agree. They are full of the old kings, sages and heroes of the Indian epics, used the way a well-read writer drops in names a learned audience will know. He doesn't throw that learning away. He puts it to work. Third, the poem of Nanda. His other surviving poem tells the story of Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother. Nanda is newly married to a beautiful wife, Sundari, and deeply in love. The Buddha brings him into the order, and Nanda is miserable, thinking only of her. The poem follows him, patiently, through longing, through a strange journey to see heavenly women, and on, step by step, until he lets go of craving altogether and finds peace. It's a poem about someone who did not want to be a monk, and how he got there anyway. Fourth, the monk who wrote. Put the pieces together and you get an unusual figure: a monk who lived by a discipline of simplicity, and who also wrote richly ornate verse. He didn't see those as opposites. A poet monk. Tomorrow, in his own words, why.
screen: `A SIGNATURE: SAKETA, SUVARNAKSHI.` · `BORN A BRAHMIN, TRADITION SAYS.` · `THE POEM OF NANDA.` · `SIMPLE ROBE, RICH VERSE.` · then, large: `A POET MONK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse aloud. Any verse you like: a line from a sacred text, a poem you remember from school, a song lyric you've always loved, or one of the scenes from these weeks said in your own words. Say it out loud, slowly, once. Listen to how it sounds in the room. Notice what changes when words leave the page and go into the air. Then sit with the quiet that follows. The bell holds the time.
Ashvaghosha himself. A monk from Saketa, brahmin-born, tradition says, who wrote the life of the Buddha and the poem of Nanda in verse. Today's word.
Your line: a poet monk. Today, notice one place where your discipline and your delight could work together instead of against each other. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

we have a short signature, a few later stories, and the poems.
his other poem tells of Nanda, who did not want to be a monk
Nanda longs for his wife, and the poem follows him step by step to peace.
Ashvaghosha set aside the old learning when he became a monk
his poems are full of epic kings and sages; he put that learning to work.

fork.setup: you're Nanda. newly married, deeply in love, and now you're a monk. all you can think about is her. what does the poem do with you?
options: sends you home in disgrace.
follows you patiently, step by step, to peace.
forgets you after one verse.
fork.reveal: the whole poem is Nanda's slow road from longing, through a journey to see heavenly women, to letting go of craving.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddhacarita was written by some anonymous monk.
what it means: it has a named author, Ashvaghosha, who signed his work, and wrote at least one other long poem.
what a scholar hears: the signature at the end of the poem of Nanda names his town, Saketa, and his mother, Suvarnakshi.

Buddhacarita (references to epic figures, e.g. canto 4 and 9)

723.title: Why a poem
723.hook: teaching through beauty: he wrote so people would stay for the teaching
723.howItsDone: Buddhist communities also teach through story, verse and art: temple murals of the Buddha's life, chanted verses, and retellings of the birth stories, often alongside plain instruction in the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashvaghosha himself, and your line: a poet monk. Did your discipline and your delight work together anywhere? Today the poet tells us, in his own words, why he wrote. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

A spoonful of honey, and under it, something bitter. It's an old trick with children: the medicine goes down because something sweet goes with it. It turns out a monk used the same picture to explain why he wrote. At the very end of the poem of Nanda, after all the longing and the journey and the letting go, Ashvaghosha steps out from behind the story and talks to the reader directly. He explains why a monk would write poetry at all.
screen: `HONEY OVER SOMETHING BITTER.` → `THE POET STEPS OUT.` → `WHY WRITE POETRY AT ALL?`

segments.voice: First, the purpose. He says the poem is about liberation, and that he wrote it not to give pleasure but to bring calm. The beauty was never the point. Second, the audience. He says he wrote in this ornate style to catch listeners whose minds are on other things. People who would never sit through a plain teaching might sit through a story with a love affair, a king, a heavenly journey, and stay long enough to hear what it was really about. Third, the honey. And then the picture: just as bitter medicine is mixed with honey so that it can be swallowed, he has mixed the teaching with poetry. Whatever in the poem is about liberation, that's the medicine. The rest, the descriptions, the music of the verse, is there to help it go down. Fourth, the gold. He asks his readers to take what leads to peace and leave the rest, the way someone panning for gold keeps the gold and lets the dust wash away. So the honey is honest about being honey. He isn't hiding the teaching. He's telling you exactly where it is. He said this about the poem of Nanda, but look back at the life we've heard these weeks with the same idea in mind. The empty saddle, the birds in one tree for a night, the dog with a dry bone, the torch of straw. Each one is honey around something hard: parting, grief, craving, and the way out. The poet hoped his listeners would stay for the beauty, and then keep the gold.
screen: `NOT FOR PLEASURE, FOR CALM.` · `FOR MINDS SET ON OTHER THINGS.` · `MEDICINE MIXED WITH HONEY.` · `KEEP THE GOLD, LET THE DUST GO.` · then, large: `BEAUTY CARRIES IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enjoy one beautiful thing mindfully. Find something beautiful within reach: light on a wall, the sound outside, the color of a cup, a plant, a face in a photo. Look at it, or listen, fully, for a few breaths. Enjoy it. Then, gently, ask what it's carrying. Maybe it says this moment won't last. Maybe it says you're here. Don't force an answer. Let the beauty be the door, and rest in whatever comes through. The bell holds the time.
Honey. The image Ashvaghosha used for his poetry: medicine mixed with honey, so the teaching can go down easily. Today's word.
Your line: beauty carries it. Today, when something beautiful stops you, stay one breath longer and ask what it's carrying. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

fork.reveal: Ashvaghosha mixes the teaching with poetry like medicine with honey, then tells readers to keep the gold and let the dust go.

724.title: The poem, closed
724.hook: the life once more, now in verse
724.howItsDone: The Buddha's life is retold again and again in Buddhist cultures: in temple murals and carvings, in festival plays and chanting, and in children's books, each telling choosing its own scenes and its own light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, honey, and your line: beauty carries it. Did something beautiful stop you, and what was it carrying? Today we close the book on Ashvaghosha's poem. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

Back in year one, the Buddha's life came to us in plain pieces: a birth, the sights on the road, a night ride, a tree, a first teaching, a last journey. This block told the same life again, slowly, through one poet's eyes. Same story. Different light. It's a little like walking a road you know by heart, but this time at dawn, with someone who stops to point at things you'd walked past. Today, before we leave the poem, one last walk down the whole road, and a look at what the verse added.
screen: `THE SAME LIFE, TOLD TWICE.` → `A KNOWN ROAD, AT DAWN.` → `ONE LAST WALK.`

segments.voice: First, the palace. A queen's dream, a birth in a grove, an old sage weeping because he won't live to hear the boy teach. A father who fills the palace with music because he is afraid. In the poem, the walls are made of love, and that's what makes them hard to leave. Second, the road out. The sights that the king tried to hide. The worms in the plowed furrow, grieved for like family. A refused request, a sleeping palace, gates that open on their own, a horse and a faithful attendant sent home. The poem lets every goodbye hurt. Third, the search and the night. Arguments from ministers, half a kingdom offered by a king, teachers who are good but not final, a bowl of milk-rice after the fasting. Then Mara with his flowered bow and his army, scattered. And a night of knowing, watch by watch, until dawn. Fourth, the turning and the end. Five old companions who rise despite themselves. Friends, fire-keepers, kings, a great ascetic arriving late. And in the Tibetan and Chinese, the rest: the last journey, the sala trees, the relics shared. That's the life, retold. What did the verse add? Not new facts, mostly. It added time to feel things. A father's fear. A wife's question. A prince's grief over worms. In the poem of Nanda, the poet said he wrote so people would stay for the teaching. All these days on one poem is a long stay. Tomorrow the path turns from the teacher to the people who followed him, beginning with two friends at a festival.
screen: `THE PALACE: WALLS MADE OF LOVE.` · `THE ROAD OUT: EVERY GOODBYE HURTS.` · `THE SEARCH, MARA, THE NIGHT.` · `THE WHEEL, THE ARRIVALS, THE END.` · then, large: `THE LIFE, RETOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: retell the life in five lines. Settle, and breathe. Then, in your head or quietly aloud, tell the Buddha's life in five plain lines, one breath each. Born a prince. Saw age, sickness and death. Left home. Woke up under a tree. Taught until the end. Use your own words if they come. Then let the lines go and sit with whatever stays. The bell holds the time.
The poem. Ashvaghosha's life of the Buddha, from the palace to the relics, told in verse so listeners would stay. Today's word.
Your line: the life, retold. Today, tell someone the five lines, or just one scene from the poem that stayed with you. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 724 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO FRIENDS AT THE FESTIVAL.`

725.title: Two friends at the festival
725.hook: Upatissa and Kolita watch a festival and suddenly find it empty
725.howItsDone: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples; in some Theravada temples images of the two stand on either side of the Buddha, and their story is told in sermons and at festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poem, closed, and your line: the life, retold. Did you tell someone a piece of the Buddha's life? Today a new block begins: the great disciples, the people who followed him. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

Same seats as last year. Same hill above the city. Same crowd, same plays, same music, same jokes landing in the same places. Two young men from good families sit side by side in the best seats, as they always do at this festival. Other years, they laughed at the funny parts and cried at the sad ones and threw gifts to the performers. This year, the jokes land, and neither of them laughs. The sad scene plays, and neither of them cries. Each one glances over and notices the other has gone quiet too.
screen: `SAME SEATS, SAME HILL.` → `THE JOKES LAND, NOBODY LAUGHS.` → `BOTH OF THEM, QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the two friends. Their names are Upatissa and Kolita. The commentaries say they were sons of brahmin families from villages near Rajagaha, close friends since childhood, each with a circle of young companions around him. Later they'll be known by other names, Sariputta and Moggallana. But not yet. Right now they're two well-off young men at a festival. Second, the silence. The commentary tells it simply. Kolita turns to his friend: you don't seem to be enjoying yourself today. What's wrong? And Upatissa answers with a question of his own: what is there to look at here? Before long, all these people, the actors, the crowd, the two of them, will be gone. And here we sit, laughing. Third, the turn. It turns out Kolita has been thinking the same thing. Neither of them talked the other into it. They arrived at the same emptiness, in the same seats, on the same afternoon. Nothing about the festival was wrong. The plays weren't worse. The music wasn't worse. What had changed was them. Fourth, the question that's left. They don't stay sad, and they don't go home and pretend. They decide, together, that they need to look for a way out of birth and death, a release that the festival can't give. And that's the end of today's story. Notice how close it sits to the prince's own. He saw an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and the palace music went flat. These two never leave their seats. The emptiness finds them in the middle of the fun. The show was empty.
screen: `UPATISSA AND KOLITA.` · `WHAT IS THERE TO LOOK AT?` · `BOTH THINKING THE SAME THING.` · `A WAY OUT, NOT A WAY HOME.` · then, large: `THE SHOW WAS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice when fun feels hollow. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a moment, recent or long ago, when something meant to be fun went flat: a party, a show, a scroll through your phone, a holiday you'd waited for. No need to judge it or fix it. Just remember the feeling, honestly. What were you hungry for that the fun couldn't give? Let the question sit without an answer. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Upatissa. One of two friends who sit through the festival they loved and find it suddenly empty, with his friend Kolita feeling the same. Today's word.
Your line: the show was empty. Today, if something meant to be fun goes flat, don't scroll past the feeling. Ask what you were really looking for. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

fork.reveal: Upatissa tells the truth, and finds his friend has been feeling the same thing.

726.title: A pact
726.hook: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other
726.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching gives great weight to good friendship; in the discourses the Buddha calls admirable friendship the whole of the holy life (SN 45.2), and in some communities monks and lay people practice in small groups who support each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Upatissa, and your line: the show was empty. Did you notice a moment when fun went flat, and ask what you were looking for? Today the two friends set out. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

Two hikers come to a fork in a trail at dusk, and they agree to split up. Whoever finds the way down first comes back for the other. It's a simple deal, and it only works if both of them would really come back. Upatissa and Kolita make a deal like that. Not about a trail, about the deepest thing they can name. They've left the festival, left their families' comforts, and gone to live as wanderers. And somewhere along the way they make each other a promise that will shape the rest of their lives.
screen: `A FORK IN THE TRAIL.` → `WHOEVER FINDS IT, COMES BACK.` → `THE TWO FRIENDS PROMISE.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. In Rajagaha lives a wandering teacher named Sanjaya, with a large following of wanderers. The two friends go forth under him. The commentaries say they learned everything he had to teach, quickly, and then asked: is there more? And there wasn't. In another discourse, Sanjaya is remembered for answers that slip away when you reach for them: asked a hard question, he would neither say yes, nor no, nor neither. For these two, that was not a place to stop. Second, the word. What were they looking for? The Vinaya uses one word for it: the deathless. In Pali, amata. Not long life. Not a heaven that might end. The deathless is a way of naming freedom from the whole round of birth and death, the thing the festival couldn't give. Third, the pact. And here it is, as the Vinaya tells it: the two of them had given their word to each other. Whoever reaches the deathless first will tell the other. That's all. No conditions. No race. No prize for winning. Just: if I get there, you'll hear of it. Fourth, why it matters. It would be easy for a seeker to turn inward and forget everyone else. These two built friendship into the search itself. Each one's freedom was tied to the other's. And notice what the pact assumes: that one of them might get there without the other, and that whoever did would not be too proud, too busy, or too far gone to come back. Tomorrow, one of them finds something, and we'll see if the promise holds.
screen: `A TEACHER WITH NO MORE TO GIVE.` · `AMATA: THE DEATHLESS.` · `WHOEVER FINDS IT FIRST WILL TELL.` · `FRIENDSHIP BUILT INTO THE SEARCH.` · then, large: `WHOEVER FINDS IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one promise to a friend. Settle, and breathe. Bring a friend to mind, someone whose good you want. Think of one small, honest promise you could make them and keep: I'll send you that book when I've read it. I'll tell you if I find a good doctor. I'll call you on Sunday. Not a grand vow. Something you will really do. Hold it, picture keeping it, and then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
A pact. Two friends, wanderers under Sanjaya, promise each other: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other. Today's word.
Your line: whoever finds it first. Today, make the promise you thought of, to the friend you thought of, and mean it. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

727.title: The verse passed on
727.hook: Upatissa hears Assaji's verse, understands, and runs to tell Kolita (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1)
727.howItsDone: Assaji's verse is recited in Buddhist communities as a summary of the teaching, and the story of the two friends is told at temples and in Dhamma talks as the beginning of the Buddha's chief pair of disciples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pact, and your line: whoever finds it first. Did you make one promise to a friend, and mean it? Today, one of the two friends finds it. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

Kolita sees his friend coming from a distance, and something has already changed. Not a word has been said yet. It's in Upatissa's face. The Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, tells the scene simply: Kolita notices that his friend looks calm and clear, and asks him straight out whether he has found the deathless, the thing they both left home to look for. And Upatissa says yes. Earlier on this path we followed Upatissa through the streets of Rajagaha behind a quiet monk named Assaji and heard the short verse Assaji gave him. Today is the other half of that morning: what Upatissa did with it.
screen: `A CHANGED FACE.` → `HAVE YOU FOUND IT?` → `YES, FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Start with where he went. Upatissa had just understood the thing he had left home to look for. He could have stayed to question Assaji. He could have gone straight to find the Buddha. Instead he went to Kolita, because that was the pact. The verse was small enough to carry at a run. In paraphrase: of things that arise from a cause, the Buddha has told the cause, and also how they cease. Next, notice what he passed on. Not his own summary. Not a better version. He gave Kolita the same lines he'd heard, and the text says that on hearing them, Kolita understood too. Same words, second friend. Then they thought of someone else. Their old teacher, Sanjaya, still led a crowd of students. So the two friends went back and invited him to come with them. He refused, and offered instead to share the leadership of his group with them. They said no to that, and left, and the Vinaya says many of his students went with them. What they had found was offered even to the teacher who had stopped being enough for them. Last, the arrival. The text says the Buddha saw the two friends coming from far off and told the monks, in paraphrase: these two will be my chief pair of disciples. Upatissa would be called Sariputta, and Kolita, Moggallana. Here's what the story keeps doing. Every person in it who finds something good turns around and hands it on. Assaji to Upatissa. Upatissa to Kolita. Both of them to their old teacher. The verse travels because nobody sits on it.
screen: `HE WENT TO KOLITA FIRST.` · `THE SAME VERSE, UNCHANGED.` · `BACK TO THE OLD TEACHER.` · `THE CHIEF PAIR ARRIVES.` · then, large: `HE RAN TO TELL HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pass on something good. Settle, and let the breath slow down. Go back over the last week and find one thing that helped you. A sentence someone said. A song. A recipe that worked. A way to fix a sticky door. Just one. Now find the person who would want it. Bring their face to mind, the way Kolita saw his friend's face before a word was said. Don't polish the thing or add to it. Decide only how it gets to them: a message, a call, a note on the counter. Then rest with the breath until the end. The bell holds the time.
Deathless. The thing Upatissa tells Kolita he has found, after hearing Assaji's short verse and understanding it. Today's word.
Your line: he ran to tell him. Today, when something good finds you, hand it to someone the same day, before it cools. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 727 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GENERAL OF THE DHAMMA.`

728.title: The general of the dhamma
728.hook: Sariputta, foremost in wisdom, who could explain what the Buddha said briefly
728.howItsDone: In Theravada communities Sariputta is honored as the chief disciple in wisdom, and his discourses in the Pali texts are studied as models of how to explain the teaching step by step.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deathless, and your line: he ran to tell him. What did you hand to someone before it cooled? Today, the friend who ran becomes the one who explains. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

A brahmin named Sela has just met the Buddha, and he is won over. He is also a practical man. A teacher this great, he reasons, must have someone at his side who carries the work forward, the way a king has a general. So, in the Sutta Nipata, Sela asks it in verse: who is your general? Which disciple follows the teacher and keeps this going? It's a fair question about any movement. Somebody has to explain the thing on the days the founder isn't in the room. The Buddha answers with one name.
screen: `SELA IS WON OVER.` → `WHO IS YOUR GENERAL?` → `ONE NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the name: Sariputta. In paraphrase, the Buddha tells Sela: the wheel of the teaching that I set rolling, Sariputta keeps rolling, the one who comes after me. That's where the picture of a general comes from. Not a battle. A wheel that needs someone to keep it moving. Later tradition turned it into a title: the general of the dhamma. Second, what he was known for. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of disciples who were foremost in one quality or another, the Buddha names Sariputta foremost in great wisdom. And in the discourses his wisdom has a recognizable shape: the Buddha says something short, and Sariputta opens it up so others can use it. Third, one scene of that. In the Samyutta Nikaya, a group of monks is about to leave for a far western country. The Buddha tells them: before you go, take leave of Sariputta. He's wise, and he helps his fellow monks. So they go to him, and he gets them ready. Out there, he says, wise people will question you. They'll ask what your teacher teaches. Answer simply: the removal of desire and lust. And if they ask, desire for what? Tell them: for the body, for feelings, for perceptions, for the rest of what we take ourselves to be. One plain line first, then the next step only if someone asks for it. That is the general at work: not commanding, but equipping. Looking back over this week, from the end of the poem to the start of the disciples: Ashvaghosha himself, honey, the poem closed, Upatissa, a pact, deathless, and today, the one who explains.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain one thing clearly. Settle, and breathe. Choose something you understand well. How to make rice. Why your team uses a certain tool. What a word in this path means. Now, silently, explain it the way Sariputta coached the travelers: one plain sentence first. Stop there. Imagine someone asking, what do you mean? Give the next sentence. Then stop again. If you notice yourself reaching for a long speech, come back to the breath, and to one plain sentence. The bell holds the time.
Sariputta. The disciple the Buddha named, when Sela asked who kept the wheel of the teaching rolling, foremost in wisdom, who readied others to explain it simply.
Your line: wisdom explains. Today, when someone asks you something, give one plain sentence, then wait to see if they want the next. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.
